title: Kiro Alternatives: What to Use Instead
summary: Kiro alternatives compared on what they write before code and how they bill: OpenSpec, Spec Kit, Traycer, Zenflow, Cursor, Claude Code and more.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Four of the nine Kiro alternatives after ours name more than one core planning document before code, as Kiro's feature specs do: OpenSpec and Traycer four, GitHub Spec Kit and Zenflow three.
- The other five write a single plan, and Kiro has a light Plan mode of its own, so choosing them comes down to price and editor, not planning depth.
- By our arithmetic, every paid individual Kiro tier costs $0.02 per credit, while add-on credits and pooled team credits cost $0.04, twice as much.
- OpenSpec and Spec Kit are free MIT toolkits, so their spec files cost only what the agent running them costs.


If you're searching for Kiro alternatives, you probably like Kiro's idea and dislike its bill. Planning before an agent codes makes sense, but Kiro charges in credits, multiplies them for top models, and its own docs say feature specs don't suit every job.


So this list asks two things of every tool: what it writes before code, and how it charges you. Prices are as of November 13, 2026.


First on the list is[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) , because it's our product; it publishes no spec workflow, so read its cons first. The other nine follow by how many core planning documents each tool's workflow overview names before code (four, then three, then one plan). Ties go to the cheaper paid plan billed monthly, free-only tools first, then alphabetical order.


## Why Kiro users look elsewhere


Kiro is AWS's agentic IDE, and spec mode is why people try it. A feature spec writes` requirements.md` in EARS notation, then` design.md` and` tasks.md` into` .kiro/specs/` , and Kiro runs independent tasks in concurrent "waves".


Kiro isn't spec-or-nothing, though. Bugfix Specs swap` requirements.md` for a` bugfix.md` and still write` design.md` and` tasks.md` , while Plan mode plans a change without the formal documents. The complaints we found are about cost and fit more than the idea of specs.


### Credits go faster than the plan suggests


Kiro's individual plans scale in a straight line: Pro is $20 for 1,000, Pro+ $40 for 2,000, Pro Max $100 for 5,000 and Power $200 for 10,000. By our arithmetic, that's $0.02 per credit on every paid tier. Plan credits don't roll over, and add-on credits cost $0.04 each and expire after 12 months.


Model choice then multiplies the spend. Against Auto at 1x, Kiro's models page lists Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 1.3x, Opus 5.5 at 2.0x and GPT-5.6 Sol at 4.4x, while the cheapest open-weight models go as low as 0.05x.


In an r/kiroIDE thread titled[Kiro Usage](https://www.reddit.com/r/kiroIDE/comments/1xjfl34/kiro_usage/) , a $20 Pro user on Sonnet 5.5 reported about 1.8 credits for one short planning question, and several replies called the limits unforgiving. That's anecdotal, and Sonnet's 1.3x multiplier explains part of it; other r/kiroIDE users say Auto stretches credits further.


### Pooled team seats work out at twice the per-credit price


On November 4, 2026, Kiro launched credit pooling for teams: $20 per seat buys 500 pooled credits, which is $0.04 a credit on our math, double the individual plan rate, and extra pooled credits also cost $0.04. Individual tiers stay for solo developers, but Kiro's FAQ says new Enterprise customers buy pooling seats.


### Full specs don't suit exploratory work


Kiro is candid about where feature specs fit. Its docs call them not ideal for "Bug fixes (use Bugfix Specs instead)" and "Exploratory coding without clear goals", and Quick Spec trims the ceremony by writing all three files in one pass with no approval gates. What still bites is the meter: a spec task typically costs more than 1 credit, and spec refinement and hook runs draw credits too.


Workflows drag as well. In[another r/kiroIDE thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/kiroIDE/comments/1x31rk1/am_i_using_kiro_wrong_or_does_it_feel_painful_to/) , a user building a simple RSVP site said workflows looped and sub-agents asked for approval so often they couldn't step away, and one reply called Kiro "not great for prototyping from scratch". That's one user, and the complaint is about workflows, not spec files.


### One vendor's tools


Kiro's IDE is a Code OSS fork, its CLI, Web and mobile apps are Kiro-only as well, and JetBrains works only through the Agent Client Protocol, with no Visual Studio or Eclipse plugin. Routing a subscription through third-party automation harnesses outside Kiro's own interfaces isn't permitted either. If the editor is what you want to replace, our[Windsurf alternatives roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/windsurf-alternatives) covers other AI editors.


## The best Kiro alternatives, compared


The last column carries this list's argument: what each tool writes before code, in its vendor's words. Pricing shows any free tier, then the cheapest monthly paid plan.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Read that column against your own work, not as a score. In our view, four documents pay off on a feature several people will review, and one plan is plenty for a bug fix.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Choosing the agent for each job


**Overview:** Kiro gives you one vendor's agent and its spec flow. We start at the other end: you pick the agent for each job from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode and run several at once, one chat each, on the same project files.


Every agent works on a cloud computer that belongs to the project, holds up to 1 TB, and keeps working while you're offline. Models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI, plus open-source GLM and Kimi, share one bill.


Some features stall because nobody has decided what they should do. A vetted developer on a separate Dedicated expert plan can take those on from the same chat: just 0.82% of applicants pass our vetting, and we can match you in as little as 24 hours.


You can follow along in the browser, in desktop apps for macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows (x64) and Linux, or in our iOS and Android apps.


**Key features:**


- Your own MCP servers, next to 1,400+ app automations.
- A lead agent that can split a big job across a team of agents.
- Shared team keys that a teammate's agents can call without ever seeing them.
- Per-person model and budget limits, with spend by person and by model.


**Pricing:** Each agentic plan is billed per person each month, and its price is that person's AI budget: Light $19, Basic $99, Pro $199 and Studio $499. They bill monthly with no refunds, and unused budget resets. A Dedicated expert is a separate subscription priced on a call, with one Light subscription included.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**Pros:** Four agents on one bill, parallel chats on shared files, a project computer that keeps working, a vetted developer on a separate expert plan


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Start on Pro, or on Light to test the agents first.
2. Open a project and connect GitHub.
3. Describe the feature: goal, limits, what done looks like.
4. Run two agents on separate parts of it and compare their work.
5. Share the project with a link so a teammate can review it.


**Why it's a good Kiro alternative:** You trade one vendor's spec flow for four agents you can test against each other on the same files.


**Final verdict:** Choose Awesomic to run several agents on one bill, not to cut costs. If you need a developer more than agents, start on a Dedicated expert plan and check the checkout total. If Kiro's requirements, design and tasks files were what you liked, OpenSpec or GitHub Spec Kit gives you those free inside an agent you already pay for.


To try the agents on your own code,[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) on Pro.


### 2. OpenSpec


**Overview:** OpenSpec is one of the nearest things to Kiro's spec mode that doesn't ask you to switch editors, down to its` design.md` and` tasks.md` . It's a free, MIT-licensed toolkit from Fission AI that installs into an assistant you already use.


Run` /openspec-propose` and it writes four documents per change before any code:` proposal.md` , a` specs/` folder,` design.md` and` tasks.md` , all under` openspec/changes/<name>/` . The README calls the approach "fluid not rigid" and "built for brownfield not just greenfield", meaning it works on codebases that already exist, not only new projects.


**Key features:**


- Explore, propose, apply and archive commands that take a change from idea to archive.
- Plain markdown specs that live in your repo next to the code.
- Skills for "30+ AI assistants", so a spec can move between agents later.


**Pricing:** OpenSpec costs nothing and has no paid plan. The agent it runs in bills you separately.


**Pros:** Free under MIT, four planning documents per change, no new editor to learn


**Cons:** No editor or models of its own, the npm install needs Node.js 22.12.0 or newer, telemetry is on until you opt out with one config command


**What it keeps from Kiro:** The spec files, without a second credit meter on top of your agent's.


**Final verdict:** Pick OpenSpec if Kiro's spec files were the part you liked and its credits were the part you didn't.


### 3. Traycer


**Overview:** Traycer is a planning layer that sits above your coding agents rather than replacing them. It supports 22 coding agents and model providers, and 19 of those agents, Kiro among them, can run side by side in separate worktrees.


Planning a feature runs through four skills, each producing an artifact you can comment on: an epic brief, core user flows, a technical plan and a ticket breakdown. Only then does` traycer-execute` build from the tickets on agent subscriptions you already have, so Free doesn't meter tokens.


**Key features:**


- Comments on every plan artifact, plus an optional critique pass.
- Specs and tickets shared across a team on the Sync plan.
- A mobile app for reviewing plans away from your desk.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0 with cloud sync and unlimited agent sessions, and Sync, needed only for team sharing, is $16 per user per month billed yearly, or $20 monthly. Optional pay-as-you-go credits cost $1 each and are spent at the upstream API price plus 20%.


**Pros:** Free for individuals with no token metering, keeps Kiro as one of its agents, a review loop on every plan


**Cons:** Model use is separate (optional credits at API price plus 20%, or your own agent plan), its docs require an agent that can run skills such as Claude Code or Codex, team sharing needs Sync


**Where it pulls ahead:** Different agents build from the same tickets, so you can compare them on real work.


**Final verdict:** Choose Traycer if you already pay for two coding agents and want one reviewed plan feeding both.


### 4. GitHub Spec Kit


**Overview:** Spec Kit is GitHub's own MIT-licensed take on spec-driven development. You drive it with slash commands in your agent's chat:` /speckit-specify` writes` spec.md` ,` /speckit-plan` writes` plan.md` and` /speckit-tasks` writes` tasks.md` , and` implement` builds from them.


Spec, plan and tasks are its three core planning files per feature, though the plan step also writes` research.md` ,` data-model.md` ,` contracts/` and` quickstart.md` . The count leaves out` /speckit-constitution` , which you run once per project to set its principles, and the optional` clarify` ,` checklist` and` analyze` steps.


**Key features:**


- A read-only` analyze` step that cross-checks spec, plan and tasks.
- Extensions, presets and workflows for building your own process.
- Bundled processes for bug fixes and for assessing new ideas.


**Pricing:** Spec Kit is free under MIT, with no paid plan. Your only cost is the coding agent you run it in.


**Pros:** Free, maintained by GitHub with a release as recent as November 10, 2026, works across many agents


**Cons:** A toolkit rather than an IDE or a model, the README asks you to run each step "one at a time, reviewing each result"


**Why it works as a Kiro alternative:** You keep a Kiro-like spec, plan and tasks rhythm, and the one-time constitution holds project-wide rules much as Kiro's steering files hold project context.


**Final verdict:** Choose Spec Kit for Kiro-style spec structure at no cost, as long as you don't mind driving each step yourself.


### 5. Zencoder Zenflow


**Overview:** Zenflow is the closest paid match to Kiro here. A full run moves through four stages that write` requirements.md` ,` spec.md` and` plan.md` , and an AI verifier checks each step's diff against the spec before the next step starts.


Zencoder doesn't force that process on small jobs. Its docs reserve the full workflow for features touching 5 or more files or multiple services, or needing stakeholder review, and send one-sentence tasks under 10 minutes to Quick Change, much as Kiro keeps vibe mode for unplanned work.


**Key features:**


- A verifier that compares each step's code changes with the spec.
- Several agents running in parallel inside one workflow.
- A desktop app plus IDE plugins.


**Pricing:** Pro is $45 per user per month, or $40 billed annually, with 30,000 credits, and bring-your-own-key use doesn't touch them. A Free plan runs on bring-your-own-key only, with no bundled credits, and there's a 7-day Pro trial.


**Pros:** Requirements, spec and plan files, a verifier on every step, bring-your-own-key on every plan


**Cons:** No bundled credits on Free, credits per seat give no clear cost per task, the full workflow is meant for bigger changes


**What the extra cost buys:** A second check on every diff, so drift from the spec shows up mid-run instead of at code review.


**Final verdict:** Pick Zenflow for multi-file features where a spec check after each step is worth $45 a month, or $40 billed annually.


### 6. Cursor


**Overview:** Cursor starts in the straight-to-code camp and gives you a brake when you want one. Press Shift+Tab and Plan Mode asks clarifying questions, researches your codebase and drafts a plan you can edit in chat or as markdown before the agent writes anything.


Plans save to your home directory unless you choose "Save to workspace". It's one document rather than three, so you swap Kiro's structure for speed on everyday changes.


**Key features:**


- Plan Mode with an editable markdown plan.
- Cloud agents and automations on Premium.
- Bugbot code review on Premium.


**Pricing:** Free is limited, Plus is $8 a month, or $80 a year, with Grok and Cursor's Composer models only, and Premium is $30 for four times Plus usage, with third-party models billed on top at API list price. Cursor joined SpaceX on August 14, 2026, and its pricing page says subscriptions are sold only through X Subscription Corp.


**Pros:** An editable markdown plan, an $8 paid plan that's the cheapest here, a familiar editor


**Cons:** Plus runs only Grok and Composer models, third-party model use costs extra on top of Premium, a new owner and a bundled X subscription


**The planning upside:** The plan is one markdown file you edit before any code, and you decide whether it goes into the repo.


**Final verdict:** Choose Cursor if most of your work is small changes and you want a plan only when a task earns one.


### 7. GitHub Copilot


**Overview:** Copilot's planning lives in VS Code's Plan agent. Type` /plan` and it researches the project, asks clarifying questions and returns a plan listing steps, affected files and how to verify the work. In the current Copilot harness, "Open Full Plan" opens the plan file in the Markdown editor, and you save a separate copy to keep it with the project.


**Key features:**


- A Plan agent that names files and checks before any edit.
- Agent mode and the Copilot CLI on all plans.
- Copilot in the cloud, beside the editor and the CLI.


**Pricing:** Free gives "Limited chat and agent usage", Pro is $10 per user per month with $15 of included AI credit value, and Pro+ is $39 with $70. The plans page shows no annual option.


**Pros:** A $10 entry price, planning inside VS Code, a free plan


**Cons:** Agent work draws down AI credits, you save a copy to keep a plan with the project, the older Local harness in VS Code, which kept plans in session memory, is deprecated and goes away in February 2027


**Its strongest case:** Planning arrives inside the editor you already run, so trying it costs one slash command.


**Final verdict:** Choose Copilot for light planning inside VS Code at $10 a month.


### 8. Qoder


**Overview:** If you've read that Qoder is spec-driven, check the date. Its Quest window, which held a Spec toggle for requirements, a design plan, a task breakdown and acceptance criteria, was retired on October 15, 2026.


What Qoder offers now is Plan mode:` /plan` , or Shift+Tab on macOS, produces a plan you review, and the save dialog defaults to` .qoder/specs` , a Kiro-like folder habit without Kiro's three files.


**Key features:**


- Plan and Goal modes, with your approval as the handoff between them.
- A codebase knowledge base the agent works from.
- An app, IDE, JetBrains plugin and CLI in one product family.


**Pricing:** Free includes limited completions, bring-your-own-key and a two-week Pro trial with 300 credits. Lite costs $10 a month with 1,000 credits, Pro $20 with 2,000, and unused monthly credits expire.


**Pros:** 1,000 credits for $10, a plan saved to a path you choose, bring-your-own-key on Free


**Cons:** The spec-style Quest window is gone, credits expire monthly, refunds only within 24 hours and only if no credits were used


**Where it saves money:** Bring-your-own-key on Free lets you try Qoder on your own API account before paying it anything.


**Final verdict:** Pick Qoder for cheap plan-then-build work, not for the spec workflow older reviews describe.


### 9. Google Antigravity


**Overview:** Antigravity is Google's agent family: an app, IDE, CLI and SDK. In the app and CLI,` /plan` asks questions, then drafts an Implementation Plan artifact you comment on before pressing Proceed.


On any tier,` /grill-me` can first run a Socratic interview on your design, settling requirements much as Kiro's first spec file does. On Google AI Pro or Ultra, the Orchestrator option splits the job by model, planning on Gemini 4 Argon or Carbon and executing on Hydrogen.


**Key features:**


- Inline comments on the plan before you press Proceed.
- ` /grill-me` design interviews before the plan exists.
- Separate planning and building models through the Orchestrator, on Pro or Ultra.


**Pricing:** The Individual tier is free with "Basic weekly rate limits". Google's AI plans page lists Google AI Pro at $19.99 a month, or $199.99 a year, and Ultra from $99.99 a month, billed monthly only.


**Pros:** A real free tier, a plan you can annotate,` /plan` and` /grill-me` on every tier


**Cons:** No bring-your-own-key for extra rate limits, Claude 5.5 models aren't on the free tier, and the older 4.6 ones leave it on November 18, quotas are unpublished and "subject to modification"


**The standout idea:** On Pro or Ultra, splitting planner and builder across models is a choice Kiro leaves to its multiplier table, or to Auto.


**Final verdict:** Choose Antigravity to try plan-first agents for free before you pay anyone.


### 10. Claude Code


**Overview:** Claude Code is Anthropic's coding agent, and plan mode is its built-in pause. Press Shift+Tab, or start a prompt with` /plan` , and Claude will "research and propose changes without making them": it writes a plan and leaves your source alone until you approve it or keep planning.


A setting in` .claude/settings.json` can make plan mode the default, and the same agent runs in the terminal, in IDEs, on desktop and on the web.


**Key features:**


- Plan mode as a per-prompt choice or a project default.
- Plan editing in your own editor with Ctrl+G.
- One agent across terminal, IDE, desktop and web.


**Pricing:** The Free plan doesn't include Claude Code, and Pro costs $17 a month on annual billing, or $20 monthly. Max at $100 and Ultra at $200 raise usage to 5 and 10 times Pro.


**Pros:** A plan you edit in your own editor, paid plans from $17 a month, runs in several places


**Cons:** No Claude Code on Free, plan mode isn't enforced in interactive terminal sessions where bypass permissions are available, usage limits are multiples of Pro rather than fixed counts


**What it does best:** It makes planning a default you set once, instead of a mode you have to remember.


**Final verdict:** Pick Claude Code for Claude models, planning on demand and a usage limit you don't count in credits.


## What planning before code actually buys you


The case for specs is older than AI coding. A 2004 NASA and INCOSE paper by Stecklein and colleagues on[error cost escalation](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20100036670) found that a requirements error costing 1 unit to fix in the requirements phase costs 3 to 8 units in design, 7 to 16 at build, 21 to 78 in integration and test, and 29 to more than 1,500 in operations.


The NASA figures come from spacecraft and aircraft-scale systems in 2004, so read them as a direction, not a forecast for your web app.


Closer to today's tools, Jiang and colleagues at Peking University tested planning before code generation. Their ACM TOSEM paper on[self-planning code generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06689) reports a "relative improvement of up to 25.4% in Pass@1 compared to direct code generation, and up to 11.9% compared to Chain-of-Thought code generation."


That study ran code-davinci-002 on HumanEval and MBPP, the model wrote its own plan, and "up to" is the best case. Neither paper compares four planning files with one.


Our read is that the habit matters more than the file count, which is why plan-mode tools sit on this list. It's the same habit behind[design-driven development](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/design-driven-development) : settle what you're building before anyone builds it.


## What Kiro alternatives cost per month


Prices only compare once you know the unit, so the last column shows what each plan meters.


Credits don't convert between vendors. Qoder Lite's 1,000 credits cost $10 and Kiro Pro's 1,000 cost $20, but neither defines a credit as the same work, so run one real task on each.


If Claude Code's flat subscription appeals, check its rivals in our[Claude Code alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/claude-code-alternatives) guide before you commit.


## Moving your .kiro specs and steering files


Specs and steering files are markdown, so they travel, while hooks need rebuilding. Here's a move that keeps Kiro running while you test:


1. Copy` .kiro/specs/` as it is, since its markdown files open in any agent.
2. Map each spec, on our reading: in Spec Kit,` requirements.md` roughly becomes` spec.md` ,` design.md` becomes` plan.md` and` tasks.md` stays` tasks.md` ; in OpenSpec, requirements split across` proposal.md` and` specs/` , beside` design.md` and` tasks.md` .
3. Move` product.md` ,` tech.md` ,` structure.md` and anything in` ~/.kiro/steering/` into AGENTS.md, or into Spec Kit's constitution if you chose Spec Kit.
4. Turn each hook in` .kiro/hooks/` into a manual step or a CI check, since hooks are JSON tied to Kiro events such as PostFileSave.
5. For a plan-mode tool, point the plan prompt at the copied` requirements.md` , then compare the result and the cost with Kiro's run.


Kiro reads AGENTS.md too, so both tools can share it during the trial if the new one does. Cancel once a real feature ships through the new tool.


## Spec-first or straight to code: how to choose


Choose by task, not loyalty. A feature that touches many files and goes through review earns a spec, and we'd use Zenflow's own threshold of 5 or more files as the line.


Below that line, plan mode is enough, whether that's Kiro's own Plan mode or plan mode in Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot on a different bill.


Budget decides the rest. If you already pay for an agent, OpenSpec or Spec Kit adds spec files for nothing, and Traycer suits different vendors' agents building from one reviewed plan, since Kiro's waves run Kiro's own agent.


Whichever you pick, a spec is a brief written for a machine, and the rules for[crafting a good creative brief](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/crafting-a-good-creative-brief-unlock-business-results-faster) carry over: one goal, named constraints and a clear definition of done.


## Kiro competitors we left off


A few Kiro competitors came close and lost out to the 10-entry cap: Kilo Code's plan agent writes plan files to` .kilo/plans/` , and Cline's Plan & Act has a read-only plan mode.


Verdent's plan-mode page is labeled archived 1.0 documentation, so it stays off. Augment Code's own roundup, a top search result, puts its Cosmos first, as we do ours, and we cover its rivals in our[Augment Code alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/augment-code-alternatives) roundup.


## Which Kiro alternative to try first


Start where it costs least: run one spec Kiro already wrote through OpenSpec or Spec Kit in an agent you already pay for, then do one small fix with Antigravity's free` /plan` or Cursor's Plan Mode, and compare time and spend with Kiro's.


If the spec itself is the bottleneck, a person can help. We can match you with a[vetted design engineer](https://www.awesomic.com/design-engineer) to take a fuzzy brief to production-ready code, on a separate expert plan.


## FAQ


### Is Kiro free?


Kiro's Free plan gives you 50 credits a month on open-weight models plus Claude Sonnet 4.5, with limits. A first upgrade to Pro adds the rest of that month free and 500 trial credits, and after that Pro costs $20 a month.


### Which Kiro alternatives write spec files like Kiro does?


OpenSpec and Traycer name four core planning documents before code, and GitHub Spec Kit and Zencoder Zenflow name three, as Kiro's feature specs do. Qoder retired its Quest spec window on October 15, 2026, leaving a Plan mode that writes one plan.


### Can I bring my own API key to Kiro?


We found no bring-your-own-key option for the Kiro IDE or CLI in its pricing or docs. Kiro Crew is the exception: it can run other harnesses, such as Claude Code, Codex or a DeepSeek harness, and the DeepSeek one takes your own provider keys. On this list, Zenflow allows bring-your-own-key on every plan and Qoder's Free plan includes it.


### Is Kiro open source?


Not the parts most people use. The Kiro IDE and CLI are proprietary under the AWS IP License, while Kiro Crew is Apache-2.0. On this list, OpenSpec, Traycer and GitHub Spec Kit are MIT-licensed.


### Do I need a spec for every coding task?


No, and Kiro agrees: its docs send bug fixes to Bugfix Specs and call feature specs a poor fit for exploratory coding without clear goals. If the product is still taking shape, our[SaaS product development](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/saas-product-development) guide helps you scope a first version, which settles what needs a spec.
